title: Reachy Mini goes fully local
oneSentenceSummary: This blog post provides a comprehensive, step-by-step guide to running a fully local, private voice conversation pipeline on the Reachy Mini robot using Hugging Face's speech-to-speech library and open-source models.
summary: The article details how to set up a fully local speech-to-speech pipeline for the Reachy Mini robot, eliminating the need for cloud servers and API keys. It introduces Hugging Face's `speech-to-speech` library, a cascaded pipeline (VAD → STT → LLM → TTS) that exposes a Realtime API-compatible WebSocket. The guide covers running the LLM locally with `llama.cpp` and Gemma 4, installing and configuring the speech-to-speech library, and connecting the robot. It then delves into customization, explaining the rationale for a local setup (privacy, cost, control) and offering opinionated defaults for VAD (Silero), STT (Parakeet-TDT), and TTS (Qwen3-TTS). The article extensively covers LLM options, including running models in-process with MLX or Transformers, or decoupling the brain via a Responses API with various backends like vLLM, Hugging Face Inference Endpoints, or OpenAI. It concludes with instructions for running the engine on a laptop while the app runs on the robot.

mainPoints.point: A fully local voice pipeline for Reachy Mini is achievable using open-source models and Hugging Face's speech-to-speech library.
mainPoints.explanation: The guide demonstrates a complete, private, and cost-free setup by running all components (VAD, STT, LLM, TTS) locally, removing reliance on cloud services.

mainPoints.point: The cascaded pipeline architecture offers flexibility and performance, allowing users to swap individual components.
mainPoints.explanation: The VAD → STT → LLM → TTS cascade is presented as the most flexible open-source option, enabling users to optimize for latency, quality, or language by replacing any stage with a preferred model.

mainPoints.point: Decoupling the LLM via a Responses API is the recommended approach to address the primary latency bottleneck.
mainPoints.explanation: Running the LLM in a separate process using the Responses API protocol allows for independent scaling and optimization, with support for various backends from local llama.cpp/vLLM to cloud-based providers like OpenAI.

mainPoints.point: The guide provides concrete, opinionated defaults for each pipeline stage to simplify setup.
mainPoints.explanation: It recommends specific models like Silero VAD, Parakeet-TDT STT, Qwen3-TTS, and Gemma 4 LLM, while emphasizing that these are starting points that can be swapped based on user needs.

keyQuotes: Audio never leaves your network, the entire pipeline runs on hardware you control.
Cascades are the most flexible option in the open-source landscape today, and with the right pieces they're also the fastest.
The main bottleneck in the system is LLM inference latency. To address that, we support external inference engines exposed through the Responses API protocol.
Every stage of the pipeline is a trade-off: there are faster TTS models with lower quality, slower STT models with higher quality.
